clue.text: For Cammock a holiday on the Hill

parts.note: a holiday is a rest from work
Harrow School, a famous English public school, stands on Harrow-on-the-Hill and is known as 'the Hill'

explanation.surface: Someone named Cammock is going for a break at a hilltop resort.
explanation.walkthrough: Cammock reads like a surname, but it is the old name of a wild plant. Harrow is the English public school whose pupils call it 'the Hill'.
explanation.definitionFit: Cammock is a country name for this tough-rooted pink-flowered weed of the pea family.

clue.text: Frost's poems

definitions.meaning: rime is hoar frost, so the plural means frosts
an old spelling of rhymes, short verses

explanation.walkthrough: Robert Frost the poet is the surface; the first sense is frosts, the second the old spelling of verses, as in Coleridge's Rime of the Ancient Mariner.
explanation.definitionFit: Hoar frost is rime, and the archaic spelling of rhymes, as in Coleridge's title, means verses.

clue.text: A man of rising account sits below the salt in Spain

indicators.note: sits below in a down clue puts the following pieces after the salt

parts.note: sal is the Latin and chemists' word for salt
taken as written

indicators.note: rising in a down clue means read upwards, so the abbreviation for account is reversed

explanation.surface: A man of low standing sits below the salt at a Spanish dinner table.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Below the salt' was the low-status end of a medieval table, which disguises the instruction: in a down clue 'sits below' means comes after, and 'rising' turns the account abbreviation upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: The university city of western Spain, so a place found in Spain.

clue.text: He wrote of Ahab in the main

definitions.text: He wrote of Ahab in the main

parts.words: He wrote of Ahab in the main
parts.note: not the biblical king Ahab but the whaling captain on the high seas, so the American author of Moby-Dick

explanation.walkthrough: Ahab is a king of Israel in the Bible, but 'in the main' (at sea) points to Captain Ahab of Moby-Dick and the man who wrote it.
explanation.definitionFit: The American novelist who wrote Moby-Dick, whose Captain Ahab hunts the whale across the ocean.

clue.text: Divi-man

parts.note: divi is British slang for a dividend, so a person living off dividends and interest

explanation.walkthrough: 'Divi' is British slang for a dividend, as in the Co-op divi, so the man lives on his investment income.
explanation.definitionFit: A person whose income comes from investments and dividends rather than work.

clue.text: Does it weigh on you to send work to the printers ?

parts.note: op, short for opus, means a musical work
the press means the printing works or printers

explanation.surface: An author worries about sending a manuscript off to be printed.
explanation.walkthrough: OP is the short form of opus, a work, and PRESS is the printing business.
explanation.definitionFit: To burden or crush someone is to weigh heavily on them.

clue.text: Fairy coachman's fare

definitions.meaning: in Romeo and Juliet, Mercutio says Queen Mab's chariot was made by the squirrel or 'old ...', the fairies' coachmakers

explanation.walkthrough: Mercutio's Queen Mab speech names the insect larva as the fairies' coachmaker; the second sense is the everyday slang for food.
explanation.definitionFit: The larva builds the fairy queen's coach in Shakespeare, and the same word is informal slang for food.

clue.text: He effected a tie-up with the Mores

definitions.text: He effected a tie-up with the Mores

parts.words: He effected a tie-up with the Mores
parts.note: William, who married Sir Thomas More's daughter Margaret, has a surname meaning one who ties with cord

explanation.walkthrough: William Roper married Margaret, daughter of Sir Thomas More, and wrote More's life; his surname also names a man who ties things up.
explanation.definitionFit: Thomas More's son-in-law and biographer bore a surname meaning a rope-maker, one who ties things.

clue.text: Limerick old-man's-beard

parts.note: Edward Lear's limerick about the Old Man with a beard, in which two owls, a hen, four larks and a wren all nested

explanation.walkthrough: Old-man's-beard is a wild clematis, but here it is the beard of Edward Lear's limerick, where 'Two Owls and a Hen, Four Larks and a Wren, Have all built their nests in my beard'.
explanation.definitionFit: Lear's bearded old man found his beard full of nests built by owls, larks, a hen and a wren.

clue.text: Feather-headed aubade

parts.note: an aubade is a dawn song; the feathered singer with a crested head is the farmyard rooster

explanation.walkthrough: 'Feather-headed' suggests a silly person; here it is the rooster with its comb and plumes, whose aubade (dawn song) is its morning crow.
explanation.definitionFit: The rooster's crow at daybreak is a morning song, the meaning of aubade.

clue.text: Flight from Cowes, say?

parts.note: Cowes on the Isle of Wight is said like 'cows'; a dairy round from cows, and RAF slang for a routine, easy sortie

explanation.walkthrough: Cowes is a sailing town on the Isle of Wight, pronounced 'cows', so the trip from it suggests the dairy round; airmen used the same phrase for an uneventful routine flight.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is airman's slang for a regular, uneventful sortie, named after the dawn dairy delivery round.

clue.text: If strict about money you should do well

indicators.note: about means going round, so the word for strict surrounds the money letter

parts.note: strict in manners means proper or correct
s, short for the old shilling (solidus), stands for money

explanation.surface: A thrifty person is promised success if careful with cash.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' puts S (shilling, from the Latin solidus) inside PROPER.
explanation.definitionFit: To thrive or flourish is to do well.

clue.text: Arithmetic Marie's 'confused by — how to explain briefly ?

parts.note: a sum is a piece of arithmetic

indicators.note: confused means jumbled, so the letters of the name are rearranged

parts.note: the name with its 's gives the six letters MARIES

explanation.surface: Marie is baffled by a sum and wonders how to put things concisely.
explanation.walkthrough: Here the possessive's S is a real letter of the anagram fodder, unlike the usual convention; 'confused' scrambles the whole name.
explanation.definitionFit: To give a short account of the main points is to explain briefly.

clue.text: Muffet's men ?

parts.note: Little Miss Muffet sat eating her curds and whey; a Middle Eastern people have a name said the same way

explanation.walkthrough: The nursery rhyme's Miss Muffet ate curds and whey, so 'her men' are a people whose name sounds like her food.
explanation.definitionFit: The people of Kurdistan share the sound of the soft milk lumps Miss Muffet ate.

clue.text: Flax-Ulm manufacture ?

annotationWithheld.why: Flax-Ulm manufacture ? (5): the anagram of ULM gives three of LINUM's letters; no clue word supplies IN, and the scan prints the same dash

clue.text: Late summer ahead — it's just too much!

parts.note: late in the sense of final, the most recent
a straw hat or boater is summer wear on the head

explanation.surface: The end of summer is near and someone is exasperated.
explanation.walkthrough: 'summer ahead' reads as summer coming, but it is a summer hat worn on the head, a straw boater.
explanation.definitionFit: The final burden that breaks the camel's back, the point where things become unbearable.

clue.text: The house contains one room a man can call his own

definitions.text: The house contains one room a man can call his own

parts.words: The house contains one room a man can call his own
parts.note: a home, the place a man lives and can call his own, read as a house holding a single room

explanation.walkthrough: The clue paints a one-room bachelor flat; the answer is simply the dwelling a person calls home.
explanation.definitionFit: A dwelling or home is the place where someone lives and which they can call their own.

clue.text: Then did you get your jar, Goatsucker ?

definitions.text: Then did you get your jar, Goatsucker ?

parts.words: Then did you get your jar, Goatsucker ?
parts.note: the goatsucker is the nightjar, so its 'jar' comes at dusk

explanation.walkthrough: A jar looks like a pint at the pub, but the goatsucker is the nightjar bird, and its jar comes as darkness arrives.
explanation.definitionFit: Dusk, the coming of night, is when the night bird gets its name and starts its churring.

clue.text: Swordsman agape

parts.note: not a fencer but a fairground performer who opens his mouth wide and sends a blade down his throat

explanation.walkthrough: 'Swordsman' suggests a fencer; the open mouth points to the sideshow act of taking a sword down the throat.
explanation.definitionFit: A sideshow sword act needs a performer who gulps the blade down, mouth wide open.

clue.text: Cricket washed out ? Could be a record

definitions.text: Cricket washed out ? Could be a record

parts.words: Cricket washed out ? Could be a record
parts.note: a rain-ruined test match is a ..., and record rainfall makes something the most rainy

explanation.walkthrough: A Test is an international cricket match; a rained-off one is a wet Test, and the same letters mean the rainiest, a record.
explanation.definitionFit: The superlative of rainy, used of the dampest day or year on record.

clue.text: Right amount of current with a particle of salad

parts.note: amp, an ampere, is the unit of electric current
an ion is a charged particle

explanation.surface: Someone serves just the right portion of currants with a small bit of salad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'current' looks like the fruit currant, but it is electric current, measured in AMPs.
explanation.definitionFit: A bellflower whose roots and leaves were eaten in salads, the plant Rapunzel is named after.

clue.text: Nothing commonly dutiable?

definitions.meaning: in everyday speech zero is often said as 'nought' with the n dropped
the verb of duty: what one is bound to do

explanation.walkthrough: 'dutiable' normally means liable to customs duty; here it points to the word expressing moral duty.
explanation.definitionFit: A common variant of nought means zero, and the same word is the auxiliary of obligation or duty.

clue.text: Mandatory mountain

parts.note: the peak where Moses received the commandments, the mountain of mandates

explanation.walkthrough: 'Mandatory' sounds like compulsory, or a League of Nations mandate; here it is the mountain where the Ten Commandments were given.
explanation.definitionFit: The biblical peak where Moses received the Law is the mountain of commandments.

clue.text: Such ale is not for baby

definitions.text: Such ale is not for baby

parts.words: Such ale is not for baby
parts.note: strong foaming ale is described by an old word that is also the British name for a baby's cloth wrap

explanation.walkthrough: Old strong, heady ale was called by this name; in British English it is also a baby's diaper, which is very much for baby, hence the italic 'not'.
explanation.definitionFit: An archaic word for strong, foaming ale, and the British word for a baby's diaper.

clue.text: Return thanks in places of worship for patterns of industry

indicators.note: in puts the reversed thanks inside the places of worship

parts.note: temples are places of worship

indicators.note: return means send back, so the short word for thanks is read backwards

parts.note: ta is British informal for thank you

explanation.surface: A congregation gives thanks in church for the craftsmen's designs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Return thanks' reads as saying grace, but 'Return' reverses the British slang for thanks, and 'in' tucks it into the places of worship.
explanation.definitionFit: Shaped guides used in manufacture to cut or mark identical parts are industrial patterns.

clue.text: Steps to an earldom

definitions.meaning: a flight of steps, one tread of which is a single step
the Earl of ... is a title in the Scottish peerage

explanation.walkthrough: The Earl of Stair is a Scottish title, held by the Dalrymple family.
explanation.definitionFit: A flight of steps goes by this word, and so does a Scottish earldom held by the Dalrymples.

clue.text: Check concerning the circulation rate

parts.note: re means concerning, as in a letter heading
the pulse measures the rate at which blood circulates

explanation.surface: A doctor examines a patient's heart rate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Check' looks like a medical examination, but it is the definition in the sense of drive back.
explanation.definitionFit: To drive back or halt an attack is to check it.

clue.text: Enter Miss Merion in state

parts.note: in is the call to come inside, the word for enter
Diana Merion is the heroine of George Meredith's novel Diana of the Crossways

explanation.surface: A heroine walks on stage in a dramatic condition.
explanation.walkthrough: Miss Merion is Diana Merion, heroine of George Meredith's 1885 novel Diana of the Crossways.
explanation.definitionFit: The Hoosier State is one of the fifty United States.

clue.text: The above lady's were cross

parts.note: the lady of the clue above is Meredith's Diana, whose novel's title says her paths were cross

explanation.walkthrough: The 'above lady' is Diana Merion from the previous clue; the title Diana of the Crossways says her roads, read as her habits, were cross.
explanation.definitionFit: Roads or paths, and also habits, are what the novel's title calls cross.

clue.text: On battle-winning playing fields isn't the tackling low?

definitions.text: On battle-winning playing fields isn't the tackling low?

parts.words: On battle-winning playing fields isn't the tackling low?
parts.note: Waterloo was said to be won on the playing fields of Eton; tackling an opponent is collaring him, and the school's collar is broad and low

explanation.walkthrough: Wellington supposedly said Waterloo was won on the playing fields of Eton; to collar is to tackle, and the school's wide stiff collar was worn low.
explanation.definitionFit: A broad stiff white neckband worn over the jacket by younger boys at that Thames-side school.
